B b<sup>B = flux density in fields, susceptance in AC, constant B in lines.</sup>
C c<sup>c = speed of light or specific heat. C = capacitance or the output C(s).</sup>
D = duty ratio in choppers, diameter in mechanics, spacing in lines, flux density in D d fields.
Small e = a value that changes with time (instantaneous) or a pure constant. Capital E E e = the steady value (rms or DC) or a field / modulus.
F f<sup>Small f = frequency or a function; capital F = force, mmf or F(s).</sup>
G g<sup>g = 9.81 or transconductance; G = conductance or forward gain.</sup>
H h<sup>H in stability = inertia constant (seconds), in fields = magnetising force.</sup>
Small i = instantaneous current. Capital I = rms / DC current, moment of inertia or I i luminous intensity. In EEE the imaginary unit is written j, because i is current.
J j<sup>j = √−1 in EEE; J = current density, moment of inertia in drives, or joule.</sup>
Transformer ratio: K = N₂/N₁ = V₂/V₁ in Indian books, but a = N₁/N₂ in others — they are K k reciprocals.
L l<sup>Small l = length; capital L = inductance.</sup>
M m<sup>m in alternators can be phases OR slots per pole per phase — read the formula.</sup>
N = speed in rpm or number of turns. n = speed in rps, turns per metre or number of N n samples.
P p<sup>Watch P in machine formulas — it is the number of POLES, not power.</sup>
Q q<sup>Q has five different meanings — read the subject first.</sup>
R r<sup>Small r = radius or internal resistance; capital R = resistance or gas constant.</sup>
s in induction motors = slip; s in control = Laplace variable. They never appear S s together, so check the chapter.
T t<sup>T is the busiest capital letter: period, torque, temperature, turns, tension, tesla.</sup>
U u<sup>u = initial velocity or unit step; U = internal energy or utilization factor.</sup>
V v<sup>Small v = instantaneous voltage or velocity. Capital V = rms / DC voltage, or volume.</sup>
W w<sup>w = weight per metre (sag); W = work/energy or watt. Never write w for ω.</sup>
X x<sup>Small x = variable or distance; capital X = reactance.</sup>
Y y<sup>Y = admittance, star connection, or the bus admittance matrix.</sup>
Z z<sup>Z in DC machines = number of conductors, not impedance.</sup>
α<sup>alpha · α changes meaning in almost every subject.</sup>
β<sup>beta · β = BJT gain, phase constant, feedback factor, slot angle or FM index.</sup>
γ Γ<sup>gamma · γ = ratio of specific heats or propagation constant; Γ = reflection coefficient.</sup>
delta · δ = load angle, skin depth or air density factor. Δ = delta connection, a change, δ Δ or a determinant.
ε<sup>epsilon · ε = permittivity in fields, strain in mechanics, emissivity in heat.</sup>
ζ<sup>zeta · Both letters are used for the damping ratio — same quantity, different books.</sup>
η<sup>eta · η = efficiency; also the diode ideality factor and UJT intrinsic stand-off ratio.</sup>
θ Θ<sup>theta · θ = an angle, a temperature rise, or the pointer deflection.</sup>
κ<sup>kappa · κ (kappa) is sometimes used instead of k or εᵣ.</sup>
λ Λ<sup>lambda · λ has four meanings; Λ = permeance (1/reluctance).</sup>
μ<sup>mu · µ = permeability, friction, mean, FET amplification factor — or the prefix micro.</sup>
ν<sup>nu · ν (nu) looks like v (vee) — read carefully.</sup>
π Π<sup>pi · π = 3.1416; Π = product; π-model = medium-line circuit.</sup>
ρ<sup>rho · ρ = resistivity in circuits, density in fluids, charge density in fields.</sup>
σ Σ<sup>sigma · σ = stress, conductivity, standard deviation, or the real part of s. Σ = sum.</sup>
τ<sup>tau · τ = time constant, shear stress, or torque (physics books).</sup>
phi · Biggest trap: in AC φ = phase angle (cos φ = pf); in machines φ = flux per pole φ Φ (Wb).
ψ Ψ<sup>psi · ψ = electric flux or flux linkage; Ψ = wave function.</sup>
ω Ω<sup>omega · ω = angular frequency or speed (rad/s). Ω = ohm, the unit of resistance.</sup>
Signs and numbers that appear inside formulas: Σ (sum), ∫ (integral), × (cross product), Σ √ ∫ − (Lenz), √3, 4.44.
